title: Scaling Is Not Copy-Paste
author: Jo Lein
summary: Writing during the summer season of school visits and PD, Jo Lein argues that most education leaders confuse three distinct kinds of learning transfer — application, replication, and scaling — and that this confusion, not bad intentions, is why so many good ideas fail to take root elsewhere. Application means adapting a core idea to your own context and requires judgment; replication means recreating a practice with fidelity because the conditions are similar enough that faithfulness matters; scaling means identifying the underlying conditions that made a practice powerful and letting each site build its own version that preserves those conditions while adapting the form. The piece's central diagnosis is that organizations say they want to scale but actually want to replicate — they want the exact thing that worked elsewhere copied and pasted, without re-learning the messy local conditions that made it work the first time. Lein connects each mode to a different adult-learning design (coaching and reflection for application; modeling, rehearsal, and fidelity checks for replication; principles and adaptive-expertise building for scaling) and argues that failed initiatives typically hand people something to replicate, call it scaling, train them for application, and then wonder why implementation is inconsistent.
points: Names the core confusion driving failed school-improvement initiatives: leaders say they want to 'scale' a successful practice but actually want to 'replicate' it — copy-paste the exact form without re-learning the local conditions that made it work.

Offers a clean three-way framework — application (adapt the idea, judgment-driven), replication (preserve the model, fidelity-driven), scaling (protect the essence while adapting the form, principle-driven) — each with its own diagnostic questions and adult-learning design.

The scaling example (a district identifying the five underlying conditions behind one school's strong feedback culture, then letting each school build its own version) models exactly the kind of 'find the invariant, vary the form' thinking the piece argues for.

Reframes two common leadership complaints — 'they didn't implement with fidelity' and 'that school is resisting change' — as symptoms of never having decided in the first place whether a given initiative needed fidelity or adaptation.

The punchline ('You cannot scale meaningful work by eliminating judgment. You scale meaningful work by developing judgment.') is a directly actionable reframe for any leader currently trying to roll out a practice across multiple schools or teams.
quotes: Most organizations say they want to scale. They do not. They want to replicate. They want to find the thing that worked in one place, copy it, paste it somewhere else, and get the same result without having to re-learn all the messy local conditions that made it work the first time.
Scaling means the district identifies the underlying conditions that made the practice work. Then each school builds a version that fits its size, schedule, leadership capacity, and current culture.

We blame people for "not implementing with fidelity" when we never actually figured out whether the thing needed fidelity or adaptation. We blame schools for "resisting change" when we handed them a solution built for someone else's problem.
You cannot scale meaningful work by eliminating judgment. You scale meaningful work by developing judgment.
Application is: Use the idea. Replication is: Preserve the model. Scaling is: Protect the essence while adapting the form.
Most failed initiatives give people a thing to replicate, call it scaling, offer training designed for application, and then wonder why implementation is inconsistent.
